newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore economy grew 7.0 pct in 1996 - Deputy PM.
newsitem.headline: Singapore economy grew 7.0 pct in 1996 - Deputy PM.

text.p: Singapore's economy grew by seven percent in 1996 and should "comfortably" achieve its forecast expansion of five to seven percent in 1997, Deputy Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong said on Friday.
Lee told a meeting of local business leaders that the country's economy had slowed last year "after three years of above-potential growth".

"After three to four boom years, the global electronic industry took some correction to allow the industry to shed its excessive inventory. Slower growth in regional countries also affected our hub services like shipping and entrepot trade."
Lee said the slowdown had been a welcome breather, which had allowed the economy to consolidate.

"Already, the Singapore economy has shown signs of recovery. After a weak 3.3 percent in 3Q 1996, economic growth in 4Q 1996 rebounded to 5.8 percent, better than we expected. This brings full year growth in 1996 to 7.0 percent," he said.
These figures are all higher than previous official data.
Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong said on December 31 the economy grew by 6.5 percent, an estimate in line with a recent Reuters' poll of local economists.
The government had previously said growth was 3.2 percent in the third quarter and 4.0 percent in the fourth quarter.
Lee said the prospects for the Singapore economy in 1997 were good.
"MTI (the Ministry of Trade and Industry) has earlier predicted steady growth of between five to seven percent. Judging from recent trends, we should be able to achieve this comfortably," he said.

He said a pick-up in global demand for electronics, on which around half of Singapore's industrial output and almost 60 percent of its non-oil exports depend, would flow through to Singapore "in due course".
"In recent months, U.S. new orders for electronics components have also increased, while inventory levels continued to decline," he said.
